narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. This was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Your third-year grades, which placed you in the second decile compared to an average near the sixth among accepted students, added further weight in the same direction. These early academic standings signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Working full-time, in contrast, slightly pulled the prediction toward success. Most accepted students (93%) also planned to study full-time, so this choice worked modestly in your favor.

Taken together, the model saw your low academic deciles as clear indicators that the bar exam would be difficult, outweighing the positive signal from full-time study and resulting in the 60% failure probability that led to rejection.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking key courses, or explore schools with different admissions thresholds. Improving your LSAT score and GPA could also shift future predictions in your favor.
